title: Pokémon Pokopia's Bubbly Basin DLC Dives into Risky Waters
summary:
Underwater levels in video games are almost universally dreaded. From the infamous Water Temple in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time to the clunky swimming in Super Mario 64's Jolly Roger Bay, they often mean sluggish movement, obscured vision, and a relentless oxygen timer. So when Koei Tecmo and Game Freak announced the Bubbly Basin DLC for Pokémon Pokopia during the June 2026 Nintendo Direct, it came with equal parts excitement and apprehension.

Pokopia is a cozy life sim—a genre defined by low stakes and relaxing gameplay. There's no combat, no fail states, and certainly no drowning countdown. That alone sets it apart from the frustrating underwater tropes. The new Dive move, arriving alongside the biome in August, lets players breathe indefinitely beneath the surface, opening up exploration for items, Pokémon habitats, and secrets. But the risk remains: if Bubbly Basin feels sluggish or barren, it could tarnish an otherwise charming experience.

The biome is likely inspired by Cerulean City from the Kanto region, and fans are already clamoring for it to be expansive—incorporating Routes 24 and 25, Bill's house, and even Cerulean Cave. Since Pewter, Saffron, and Vermilion Cities are already in the game, a sprawling Cerulean area seems plausible. However, the underwater content shouldn't be confined to the basin alone. The oceans surrounding Withered Wasteland, Bleak Beach, and Pallet Town need hidden caves and discoveries too, or those areas risk becoming monotonous.

One major concern is how Dive consumes PP (Power Points), the energy resource for moves. If it drains too quickly, players will be forced to surface repeatedly—a tedious interruption in an underwater-focused zone. The community is urging developers to make Dive effectively limitless, similar to how Glide works but without the constant energy drain. Another hot topic: non-water-type Pokémon. Pokopia has few restrictions on where Pokémon can live, so why shouldn't a Charmander or Carkol join the underwater neighborhood? The game's whimsical tone could easily hand-wave away the logic of fire-types submerged in water.

Bubbly Basin is a bold first expansion for a game that charmed players with its main story. Underwater levels are notoriously difficult to get right, but Pokopia's cozy nature might be the perfect antidote. If the developers listen to fan feedback—expanding the map, easing Dive's limitations, and embracing the game's playful spirit—it could be a delightful new chapter. Until then, we'll be holding our breath.
why_it_matters: This DLC tests whether a studio can break one of gaming's most stubborn tropes—that underwater zones are a chore. If Pokopia succeeds, it could inspire other designers to rethink hated gameplay conventions, showing that a calm, creative approach can turn frustration into fun. For players, it's a reminder that even established genres can evolve when developers truly understand what makes their game special.

background_read: Underwater levels have a long history of annoying players. The 1998 classic 'The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time' featured the Water Temple, a complex dungeon where slow swimming and constant equipment switching frustrated millions. 'Super Mario 64' had Jolly Roger Bay, with clumsy swimming controls and a dreaded air meter. These design choices taught gamers to expect tedium whenever they went below the surface.

Pokémon Pokopia is a 'cozy life sim'—a genre focused on relaxed activities like decorating, exploring, and befriending creatures, with no time pressure or failure states. Previous Pokémon spin-offs like 'Pokémon Snap' or 'Pokémon Ranch' also avoided combat, but Pokopia is the first to add underwater exploration through DLC (downloadable content released after the main game).

Cerulean City is the second city in the original Pokémon Red and Blue games, famous for its Water-type Gym. Bill's house, where a scientist accidentally turns himself into a Pokémon, is nearby on Route 25. The mention of these classic locations connects the DLC to decades of Pokémon nostalgia, a powerful feeling that makes older fans especially protective of how these places are represented.

perspectives.description: Cozy-game fans see the DLC as a dream come true: a new, expansive world to explore without stress. The Dive move removes the anxiety of drowning, letting players enjoy the environment at their own pace. If Bubbly Basin captures the magic of original Pokémon landmarks, it could become a fan-favorite area and justify future expansions.

Skeptics point out that underwater levels are historically boring, and a poor implementation could drag down the whole game. PP management anxiety and restrictive Pokémon placement would discourage exploration. Additionally, if the biome feels small or featureless compared to the hype, players may lose trust in the developers and abandon the game.

The tension between tradition and innovation runs through gaming history. From the Water Temple's infamy to today's cozy design philosophy, developers must balance nostalgic callbacks with modern expectations. The pushback against Dive's PP cost reflects a broader trend: players now demand that mechanics respect their time rather than create artificial difficulty.

Bubbly Basin will set a precedent for how Pokémon Pokopia handles post-launch content. If the team actively incorporates community feedback, it could build a loyal player base eager for future paid expansions. On the other hand, a half-hearted release might signal that the game will never reach its full potential, pushing fans toward competing cozy titles.
